title: Sustained throughput & energy econ audit: A10/L4/A100/H100
content:
Purpose:
This is a working audit of steady-state throughput and energy economics across four representative GPU choices (NVIDIA A10, L4, A100, H100). The goal is to produce a compact reference for routing and instance selection heuristics in Redwood Optimize: highlight $/1M-tokens, tokens/s-per-watt, and practical recommendations for common workload shapes (short-chat, long-completion, high-batch inference, embeddings).

Scope & bench target:
- Model: Llama-2-13B-v2 (community-ported checkpoint) quantized to 8-bit where possible (PTQ/QLoRA-style pipeline).
- Runtime: Triton + PyTorch backend, single-GPU tests, steady-state generation (no service-side overhead).
- Context: 2048 tokens. Samples measured are deterministic generation of synthetic prompts to avoid dataset variance.
- Metrics: tokens/s (batch=1 & batch=8), average GPU power draw (W), GPU-hour amortized cost (infra internal numbers), computed $ per 1M tokens, tokens/s per Watt (perf/W).
- Notes: numbers are relative and tied to our infra cost assumptions (see assumptions block). Use as decision guidance, not an SLA.

Assumptions used for $ calculations (amortized infra cost basis):
- A10 amortized GPU-hour cost: $0.75
- L4 amortized GPU-hour cost: $0.45
- A100 amortized GPU-hour cost: $3.00
- H100 amortized GPU-hour cost: $4.20
(These numbers include host, storage, network, and an allocation for infra ops; update when finance provides new cost curves.)

Raw summary table (single-GPU steady-state, model/quantization as above):

GPU | tokens/s (batch=1) | tokens/s (batch=8) | avg power W | tokens/s per W | tokens/hr | $ / 1M tokens
A10 | 190 | 650 | 180W | 1.06 | 684,000 | $1.10
L4  | 140 | 480 | 100W | 1.40 | 504,000 | $0.89
A100| 700 | 2600| 300W | 2.33 | 2,520,000 | $1.19
H100| 980 | 3800| 320W | 3.06 | 3,528,000 | $1.19

How numbers were derived (brevity):
- tokens/hr = tokens/s * 3600.
- $ / 1M tokens = (GPU_hour_cost) / (tokens/hr) * 1,000,000.
- power figures are the average measured package power during the steady-state run (measured with nvidia-smi sampling at 1s).
- batch scaling is empirical: for this model L4/A10 saturate memory bandwidth earlier, A100/H100 show better batch scaling.

Interpretation & takeaways (high level):
- Raw $/1M tokens is surprisingly similar between the A100/H100 and the A10: A10 wins vs A100/H100 only if you can operate in the same token/s regime per GPU. In practice, higher-throughput GPUs amortize host+sync overheads better for bursty traffic.
- L4 has the lowest $/1M in these assumptions because its amortized hourly cost is low and perf/W is good; it is the most cost-efficient for sustained, mid-throughput workloads where latency constraints are relaxed.
- H100 dominates perf/W (tokens/s per Watt) which makes it the preferable choice where power-constrained deployments (on-prem racks with tight PDU budgets) or where peak latency matters and throughput per rack is prioritized.
- A10 remains attractive as a mid-point when reserved capacity is cheaper (bulk committed pricing) or when memory footprint/compatibility with certain kernels is a factor.

Recommendations (practical heuristics for Optimize):
1) Latency-sensitive chat (turns < 256 tokens, P95 latency target <= 150ms): prefer H100 or A100 pinned endpoints with smaller batching. If cost is secondary, H100 for best latency headroom.
2) High throughput batch inference (embolized long completions or offline rerank/embeddings): favor L4 clusters for cost-sensitive, sustained jobs. Use A100 only if model size or sequence length forces A100 (memory) or when batching efficiencies push $/token below L4 in your workload profile.
3) Mixed workload routing: implement a routing policy that prefers L4 for low-cost steady-state and falls back to A100/H100 for spikes or strict SLOs. Consider a small H100 reserve pool to absorb tail-latency incidents.
4) Quantization & kernel tuning: when using 8-bit PTQ, re-run per-GPU microbenchmarks — quantization can shift ranking, and some kernels favor Ampere/Turing differently. Maintain model-specific bench records in the benchmarks repo.

Operational notes & next steps:
- Action: land a small internal benchmark job that reproduces these numbers on N-of-3 hardware per GPU family to quantify variance. Ticket: JIRA-OPT-432.
- Action: add a continuous perf/W measurement in the nightly bench pipeline and surface a perf/W delta in the console per model+variant.
- Data capture: collect 95/99p power draws and tokens/s under synthetic skewed prompt mix (short vs long) to estimate tail-costs.
- Sensitivity: re-compute $/1M tokens with alternate amortization (e.g., committed reserved pricing -20% and -40%). For some reserved-pricing cases, A100/H100 become better $/token than A10.

Risks and caveats:
- These numbers are single-GPU steady-state and omit multi-GPU sharding overhead and interconnect costs (NVLink/NVSwitch). Multi-GPU setups reduce per-token inference costs but add complexity and more fixed host-costs.
- Host/IO/networking latencies can change the practical latency/SLO tradeoffs.
- Upstream driver/Triton updates frequently change kernel efficiency. Rebench after major runtime upgrades.

Appendix: quick decision matrix (short):
- Minimum cost per sustained token (moderate model): L4
- Lowest tail-latency: H100
- Best batch scaling (large batches): H100 > A100 > A10 > L4
- Easiest dev compatibility / lowest engineering lift: A10 (older ecosystem)

Appendix: raw measurement log pointers (internal):
- Bench script: benchmarks/runs/2025-01-08/steady_state_13B_quant/
- PR with scripts and raw CSVs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/pull/101

Notes to reviewers (quick):
- This is intentionally compact and opinionated. The goal is a pragmatic reference for product routing heuristics and Optimize guidance. Please flag any disagreeing assumptions (esp. amortized GPU-hour numbers) or request extra rows (e.g., 4-bit quant, 70B models) if you want inclusion.
summary: Working audit summarizing tokens/s, perf/W, and $/1M tokens across A10, L4, A100, H100 for Llama-2-13B-v2 quantized; includes heuristics for routing and next steps.
